items.readable_text:
Content:
Recall that the cross product of two vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b}] is defined as

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b} = | \, \mathbf{a} \, | \cdot | \, \mathbf{b} \, | \cdot \sin\theta \cdot \mathbf{n},]

Content:
where

Content:
- [MATH: \theta] is the angle formed between the vectors when their tails are placed at the same point, and
- [MATH: \mathbf{n}] is a unit vector that's perpendicular to both [MATH: \mathbf{a}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b}.]

Content:
The cross product satisfies a few properties that we would normally expect multiplication to satisfy.

Content:
Specifically, given the vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a},] [MATH: \mathbf{b},] [MATH: \mathbf{c},] and any scalar [MATH: \lambda,] the following properties hold.

Content:
- The cross product distributes over addition and subtraction:
[MATH: (a ± b) × c|= a × c ± b × c; c × (a ± b)|= c × a ± c × b]
- The cross product is associative with respect to scalar multiplication:
[MATH: (λa) × b|= λ(a × b); a × (λb)|= λ(a × b)]

Content:
Let's see some examples of how we can use these properties.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we recall the following properties of the cross product:

  • The cross product distributes over addition/subtraction: [MATH: (a ± b) × c|= a × c ± b × c; c × (a ± b)|= c × a ± c × b]

  • The cross product is associative with respect to scalar multiplication: [MATH: (λa) × b|= λ(a × b); a × (λb)|= λ(a × b)]

With that in mind, let's evaluate our expression:

  • First, we use distributive property:

[MATH: (− 2a + 5b) × c|= (− 2a) × c + (5b) × c]

  • Next, we factor out the scalars: [MATH: (− 2a) × c + (5b) × c|= − 2(a × c) + 5(b × c)]

  • Finally, we substitute the given values for [MATH: \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{c}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c},] and simplify:

[MATH: − 2(a × c) + 5(b × c)|= − 2 ⋅ (i) + 5 ⋅ (− 3i + j); = − 2i − 15i + 5j; = − 17i + 5j]

items.readable_text:
Content:
The cross product depends on the order of multiplication! In other words, the cross product is not commutative.

Content:
More specifically, it is anticommutative, meaning that if we swap the order of the multiplication, the result changes sign:

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = -\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{a}]

Content:
To understand why this is so, we need to go back to the right-hand rule for calculating [MATH: \mathbf a \times \mathbf b{:}]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/9a1766ff096987b9e41ebbb09e5d4a5a]

Content:
Recall that the right-hand rule says that we calculate the direction of the vector [MATH: \mathbf a \times \mathbf b] as follows:

Content:
- First, we extend the index finger on our right hand along the direction of [MATH: \mathbf{a}.]
- Then, we extend our middle finger along the direction of [MATH: \mathbf{b}.]
- When we do this, our thumb points in the direction of [MATH: \mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/42281f1265f409cde4fd4cf57e6628ae]

Content:
We can also use the right-hand rule to calculate the direction of [MATH: \mathbf b \times \mathbf a{:}]

Content:
- First, we extend the index finger on our right hand along the direction of [MATH: \mathbf{b}.]
- Then, we extend our middle finger along the direction of [MATH: \mathbf{a}.]
- When we do this, our thumb points in the direction of [MATH: \mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a}.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/d2460a06f119dab22bb3f651b1ce5aae]

Content:
So, [MATH: \mathbf a \times \mathbf b] and [MATH: \mathbf b \times \mathbf a] have the same magnitude yet opposite direction. Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf a \times \mathbf b = -\mathbf b \times \mathbf a.]

sections.normalized_html: Find [MATH: 2\mathbf{a} \times (\mathbf{a}+3\mathbf{b})], if [MATH: \mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{a} = \mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}-2 \mathbf{k}.]
sections.readable_text: Find [MATH: 2\mathbf{a} \times (\mathbf{a}+3\mathbf{b})], if [MATH: \mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{a} = \mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}-2 \mathbf{k}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we recall the following properties of the cross product:

  • The cross product distributes over addition/subtraction: [MATH: (a ± b) × c|= a × c ± b × c; c × (a ± b)|= c × a ± c × b]

  • The cross product is associative with respect to scalar multiplication: [MATH: (λa) × b|= λ(a × b); a × (λb)|= λ(a × b)]

  • The cross product of parallel vectors equals the zero vector. In particular, [MATH: \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{a} = \mathbf{0}.]

  • The cross product is anticommutative: [MATH: a × b|= − b × a]

With that in mind, let's evaluate our expression:

  • First, we use the distributive property: [MATH: 2\mathbf{a} \times (\mathbf{a}+3\mathbf{b})=( 2\mathbf{a}) \times (\mathbf{a}) + (2\mathbf{a}) \times (3\mathbf{b})]

  • Next, we factor out the scalars: [MATH: (2a) × (a) + (2a) × (3b)|= 2(a × a) + (2 ⋅ 3)(a × b); = 2(a × a) + 6(a × b)]

  • Then, we use anticommutativity, and the fact that [MATH: \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{a} = \mathbf{0}{:}] [MATH: 2(a × a) + 6(a × b)|= 2(0) + 6(− b × a); = − 6(b × a)]

  • Finally, we substitute the given value for [MATH: \mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{a}] and simplify: [MATH: − 6(b × a)|= − 6(i − j − 2k); = − 6i + 6j + 12k]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Recall that the cross product of two vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b}] is defined as

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b} = | \, \mathbf{a} \, | \cdot | \, \mathbf{b} \, | \cdot \sin\theta \cdot \mathbf{n},]

Content:
where

Content:
- [MATH: \theta] is the angle formed between the vectors when their tails are placed at the same point, and
- [MATH: \mathbf{n}] is a unit vector that's perpendicular to both [MATH: \mathbf{a}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b}.]

Content:
The cross product satisfies a few properties that we would normally expect multiplication to satisfy.

Content:
Specifically, given the vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a},] [MATH: \mathbf{b},] [MATH: \mathbf{c},] and any scalar [MATH: \lambda,] the following properties hold.

Content:
- The cross product distributes over addition and subtraction:
[MATH: (a ± b) × c|= a × c ± b × c; c × (a ± b)|= c × a ± c × b]
- The cross product is associative with respect to scalar multiplication:
[MATH: (λa) × b|= λ(a × b); a × (λb)|= λ(a × b)]

Content:
Let's see some examples of how we can use these properties.

---

Item 2 — Example: Calculating Cross Product Expressions Using the Distributive Laws

Example Prompt:
Find [MATH: (-2\mathbf{a}+5\mathbf{b}) \times \mathbf{c},] if [MATH: \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{i}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c} = -3\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we recall the following properties of the cross product:

- The cross product distributes over addition/subtraction:
[MATH: (a ± b) × c|= a × c ± b × c; c × (a ± b)|= c × a ± c × b]
- The cross product is associative with respect to scalar multiplication:
[MATH: (λa) × b|= λ(a × b); a × (λb)|= λ(a × b)]

With that in mind, let's evaluate our expression:

- First, we use distributive property:

[MATH: (− 2a + 5b) × c|= (− 2a) × c + (5b) × c]

- Next, we factor out the scalars:
[MATH: (− 2a) × c + (5b) × c|= − 2(a × c) + 5(b × c)]
- Finally, we substitute the given values for [MATH: \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{c}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c},] and simplify:

[MATH: − 2(a × c) + 5(b × c)|= − 2 ⋅ (i) + 5 ⋅ (− 3i + j); = − 2i − 15i + 5j; = − 17i + 5j]

---

Item 5 — Tutorial: The Anticommutativity Property

Content:
The cross product depends on the order of multiplication! In other words, the cross product is not commutative.

Content:
More specifically, it is anticommutative, meaning that if we swap the order of the multiplication, the result changes sign:

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = -\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{a}]

Content:
To understand why this is so, we need to go back to the right-hand rule for calculating [MATH: \mathbf a \times \mathbf b{:}]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/9a1766ff096987b9e41ebbb09e5d4a5a]

Content:
Recall that the right-hand rule says that we calculate the direction of the vector [MATH: \mathbf a \times \mathbf b] as follows:

Content:
- First, we extend the index finger on our right hand along the direction of [MATH: \mathbf{a}.]
- Then, we extend our middle finger along the direction of [MATH: \mathbf{b}.]
- When we do this, our thumb points in the direction of [MATH: \mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/42281f1265f409cde4fd4cf57e6628ae]

Content:
We can also use the right-hand rule to calculate the direction of [MATH: \mathbf b \times \mathbf a{:}]

Content:
- First, we extend the index finger on our right hand along the direction of [MATH: \mathbf{b}.]
- Then, we extend our middle finger along the direction of [MATH: \mathbf{a}.]
- When we do this, our thumb points in the direction of [MATH: \mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{a}.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/d2460a06f119dab22bb3f651b1ce5aae]

Content:
So, [MATH: \mathbf a \times \mathbf b] and [MATH: \mathbf b \times \mathbf a] have the same magnitude yet opposite direction. Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf a \times \mathbf b = -\mathbf b \times \mathbf a.]

---

Content:
EXPLANATION
